readerTitle: The button that leads nowhere, on purpose
caseNote: 가상 사례 (골판지 상자 제조 공장, 프로젝트 관리 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 관심이 있는지 묻지 말고, 아직 없는 제품의 '문'을 실제 고객 앞에 달아 두고 몇 명이 열어 보려 하는지 센다.
misconception: 고객이 설문에서 '쓰겠다'고 답하면 수요가 있다는 뜻이다. 수요를 알려면 먼저 만들어 봐야 한다.

sources.text: 린 스타트업 실무에서 널리 쓰는 일반 개념 (fake door / painted door test)
Savoia, A. (2019). The Right It. HarperOne. ('Fake Door' 프리토타입 소개, 배경 참고용)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산: 클릭 18 ÷ 주문 페이지 방문 고객 1,200 = 1.5%, 연락처 남김 9 ÷ 1,200 = 0.75%. 설문 '쓰겠다' 45%는 가정값입니다.
Savoia의 책에 'Fake Door' 기법이 소개되어 있는지 게시 전 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드 본문에는 인용하지 않았습니다.
고객을 속이는 표시나 결제를 받는 방식은 국가별 소비자 보호 규정에 걸릴 수 있어 카드에서는 '돈을 받지 말고 바로 사실을 알린다'는 원칙만 다뤘습니다. 법률 조언은 하지 않습니다.

cards.title: The button that leads nowhere, on purpose
body: You click "Same-day delivery" on a supplier's order page. Instead of a form, you see: *"We don't offer this yet. You've just helped us decide whether to."*
It feels like a dead end. For the business, your click was the most honest answer it could get.

image.label: A door painted on a brick wall with a hand reaching for the handle
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 벽돌 벽에 그려진 문, 손 하나가 손잡이를 잡으려는 순간. 문 위에 작은 'Coming soon' 표지. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Should you buy the $80,000 printer?
body: Your plant makes plain shipping boxes for small online shops. A machine for custom-printed boxes would cost about $80,000. In a survey, many customers said they'd like printed boxes.

options.text: Call your top 20 customers and ask how often they'd order
options.feedback: You'll learn their reasons, which is useful. But you're still collecting opinions, and people are generous with yes when it costs them nothing.

options.text: Add a "Custom printed boxes: get a price" button to your order page and count clicks for three weeks
options.feedback: Cheap and fast, and it measures what customers do at the moment they order. You give up some detail, and you must tell clickers honestly that it's not ready.

options.text: Lease the machine for a year to test it properly
options.feedback: You'd learn the most, but you pay for the answer before knowing the question is worth asking. A year of lease costs can sink a small plant.

cards.title: Most said yes. Few walked through the door.
body: Over three weeks, 1,200 customers used the order page. Only 18 clicked the button. It led to: *"We don't make printed boxes yet. Want us to tell you if we do?"* Nine left their details.
The plant now had nine serious leads, not hundreds. Its next step: talk to those nine before buying anything.

image.label: Fake-door funnel: talk is wide, click is a slit
image.brief: Funnel infographic 45 said yes, 1.5 clicked, 0.75 left details.

cards.title: Fake door tests
body: A **fake door test** puts the entrance to an offer in front of real customers before the thing behind it exists. Then you count how many try to walk through.
It works because it swaps a question (*"Would you use this?"*) for an action taken in the middle of a real decision. Saying yes is free. Clicking while you're busy ordering means something.

image.label: Two paths: a speech bubble saying yes versus a hand pressing a button
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽: 'Would you use it?'에 'Yes!' 말풍선이 잔뜩. 오른쪽: 주문 화면 속 버튼을 누르는 손 몇 개만. 오른쪽 숫자가 작지만 더 선명하게 강조됨.

cards.title: Five steps to a fair test.
body: A fake door is only as good as its setup.
list: **One offer per door:** test printed boxes, not printed boxes plus faster delivery
**Real moments:** place it where customers already make decisions
**Decide the bar first:** write down what click rate means "go"
**Be honest at once:** the next screen says it isn't ready
**Follow up:** the people who clicked are your first interviews
cards.callout: Set the bar before you look, or any number will look like a yes.

cards.title: A door can be a line on a price sheet.
body: Fake doors aren't only digital. A freight company can add "weekend pickup: ask us" to its rate sheet. A bakery can chalk a new cake on the board with "order for Friday." Then count who asks.
One detail changes what you learn: **the price**. A door with no price measures curiosity. A door that shows $1.20 per printed box measures something much closer to demand.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the door is often a menu item or a plan on the pricing page, shown to a small share of users so you can compare them with everyone else.

cards.title: Every click is a small disappointment.
body: Someone wanted something and got a "not yet." Do that to a few customers for a short time and most won't mind. Leave the door up for months and trust wears thin. Never take money or promise a date.
Also, a click is interest, not a purchase. A low number can mean the button was hard to see, not that no one cares. A high number still needs a stronger test, like asking people to pay in advance.

cards.title: Now it's a project management app.
body: Your app helps small agencies track projects. Users keep mentioning syncing invoices to accounting software. Building it would take your team about three months.

options.text: Show a "Sync to accounting" menu item to 10% of users for two weeks, with an honest "not ready yet" screen and an early-access sign-up
options.feedback: Small, short and honest, with a group to compare against. You only learn interest, so plan a follow-up with the people who sign up.

options.text: Show the menu item to every user and keep it up until enough clicks come in
options.feedback: You'll get plenty of data, but every user keeps hitting a dead end with no end date. Trust erodes, and you never set a bar for "enough."

options.text: Email all users asking whether they'd use an accounting sync
options.feedback: Quick and polite, and replies can explain why. But it measures opinions, which run far higher than real use.

cards.title: Build the door before the room.
body: Before you build, put the entrance in front of real customers and count who tries to walk in. Be honest with everyone who does.
**Try it today:** pick one idea you've been asked about. Write where its door could go, what it would say, and what number would make you build it.
